title: The Iran War Turns Six Months Old as Washington Wages Economic War on Every Front
subhead: The US-Iran conflict passed its six-month mark with no off-ramp, as Washington pivoted decisively from airstrikes to a coordinated economic-isolation campaign — secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners, a nationwide arms embargo push on Sudan, and a sweeping Venezuela oil deal that would hand Washington control of 65 billion barrels. The week also saw the US-Canada trade war escalate into symbolic territory, a Himalayan glacial flood kill more than 570, and a direct US-Russia intelligence channel reopen even as the Ukraine air war turned deadlier.

sections.heading: Six Months In, the Iran War Becomes an Economic Siege
sections.body:
The US-Iran war crossed its six-month mark on Friday having outlasted every official forecast — President Trump initially predicted it would last four to five weeks. The June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding that briefly paused hostilities has expired, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Thursday that 'no negotiations are happening right now.' The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than one-fifth of global oil and gas once passed, has been largely closed since early March, with traffic down roughly 95 percent.

What changed this week is the instrument. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC Washington is preparing to 'squash' the Iranian economy and 'collapse this regime,' warning allies that 'you are either with us or against us.' He then unveiled a new wave of sanctions on nearly 60 individuals and entities under a campaign he called the 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran — 'Operation Economic Outcast' — targeting five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, and reaching across the Middle East, China, Singapore, Hong Kong and Europe. The measures now include secondary sanctions on countries that continue to do business with Tehran, forcing third states to choose between the US financial system and trade with Iran. The Iranian rial slid to 2.02 million to the dollar as trading opened Monday.

Tehran is feeling the squeeze and saying so publicly. President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that sanctions and the US naval blockade had caused exports and imports to slump by nearly 35 percent, while acknowledging Iran had managed to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the brief MoU window. Yet the leadership is not conceding the strait: the deputy foreign minister said Iranian forces retain 'full oversight' of movements in Hormuz and that Tehran is 'in no rush' to reopen the waterway. Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since the war began, issued a written statement calling on the government to address inflation, unemployment and market pressures.
sections.whyItMatters: The pivot from airstrikes to economic warfare lowers the immediate odds of a shooting war but raises the stakes of a prolonged attritional standoff. With Hormuz closed, US munitions depleted and Tehran publicly admitting a one-third collapse in trade yet refusing to yield the strait as leverage, the coming weeks will determine whether the conflict de-escalates or hardens into a longer economic siege.

sections.heading: Mediators Converge on Tehran as a Diplomatic Track Flickers Back to Life
sections.body:
Alongside the economic squeeze, a flurry of high-level visits to Tehran suggested a renewed push for talks. Qatar's Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani arrived Thursday to discuss de-escalation and reviving failed negotiations, following visits by Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir — his third trip to Iran this year — and Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi. Pakistani officials said 'significant progress' was made in talks aimed at ending the war, with discussions focused on preventing further escalation, reopening Hormuz and restoring the expired Islamabad MoU. Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping route through the strait, and Qatar has stressed the need for the waterway to return to its pre-February 28 status.

The most striking signal came from Washington's own backchannel. The New York Times reported that the CIA director made a secret visit to Moscow, and Trump acknowledged the trip publicly, telling reporters that 'something may come of' it while describing the visit as 'semi-routine.' The disclosure comes as Bloomberg reports Putin is moving to escalate the war in Ukraine with negotiations at a dead end, and the Wall Street Journal describes the Russia-Ukraine air war as having entered a new, deadlier phase. A direct US-Russia intelligence channel — acknowledged by the White House — is the most concrete sign in months that both capitals are preparing for some form of managed contact, even as the shooting war intensifies.
sections.whyItMatters: Pakistan has become the indispensable intermediary in a war with no direct US-Iran channel, and its claim of progress — alongside the Qatari and Omani visits — offers the clearest sign yet that a diplomatic track, however fragile, remains alive. The CIA's Moscow trip, meanwhile, suggests Washington is quietly opening multiple channels at once, even as it escalates economically.

sections.heading: The Iran War's Hidden Cost: NATO's Missile Defenses Are Hollowed Out
sections.body:
The war's cost to the wider Western alliance became visible this week. The US military is experiencing a 'beyond critical' shortage of advanced missile interceptors in Europe, largely driven by the war with Iran, a US defense official in Europe and a NATO official told the Associated Press. The most concerning shortfall involves Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles. US missile stocks in Europe have been moved to the Middle East, where US and Gulf allies have fired significant numbers of interceptors to thwart Iranian drones and missiles.

The officials warned that in the event of a Russian ballistic missile assault on a NATO target, the alliance could be forced 'to take punch after punch in the mouth,' in the words of the US defense official, and would have 'very limited' capability to defend against even a single ballistic missile strike. Though a Russian attack on NATO is not imminently expected, the shortfall exposes a vulnerability in European air defense at a moment when the CIA director's secret trip to Moscow has opened a new channel between Washington and the Kremlin. The drawdown is a direct consequence of the Iran war's appetite for interceptors — a strategic trade-off that has quietly shifted the balance of deterrence in Europe.
sections.whyItMatters: The Iran war has quietly hollowed out NATO's missile defense in Europe, creating a strategic vulnerability Moscow could exploit and that will take years of production to repair. It is the clearest example yet of how the Gulf conflict is degrading Western capacity to deter Russia — the two wars now share a single, depleted arsenal.

sections.heading: The US-Canada Trade War Moves From Tariffs to Territory
sections.body:
The rupture between Washington and its closest ally deepened through the week. The US imposed 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian products, and Canada said it would retaliate beginning 8 September after last-ditch negotiations collapsed. Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended talks with President Trump rather than accept a deal he said the US 'asked too much' and 'offered too little' for, accusing Washington of a 'power play' with eleventh-hour changes. Carney, one of the first world leaders to walk away from the negotiating table with the White House, told reporters 'you're at war when you're attacked — we got attacked.' Trump responded that Canada wants the 'benefits' of being a US state.

The dispute then escalated into symbolic territory. Trump signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to rename Lake Ontario 'Lake America' in US geographic naming records. Carney rejected the renaming, invoking the lake's Indigenous roots and noting the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. AP notes Canada's governing party in Quebec has named Trump its 'real adversary' as a provincial election begins, and Canada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray. Canada sends roughly 70 percent of its exports to the US, and states including Michigan, Kentucky, Indiana and Ohio are the most exposed to the fallout.
sections.whyItMatters: A dispute with Washington's closest ally and largest trading partner has moved from tariffs to symbolic territorial gestures, underscoring how far the US-Canada relationship has deteriorated. Carney's gamble that Canadians will accept economic pain to stand up to Washington is being watched closely by other governments facing Trump's pressure tactics.

sections.heading: Washington's Venezuela Gambit: 65 Billion Barrels and a Hedge Against Hormuz
sections.body:
President Trump announced Friday that his administration has reached a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that he called 'THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY.' According to AP, the deal was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez. Venezuela's government said it covers 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels, could draw $100 billion in investment and yield over $209 billion in taxes for Caracas.

Under the contours described by a US official quoted by AP, Washington would partner with an unnamed private operator to create a new company that would hold the reserves, with Rodriguez granting the firm 100-year development rights. The United States would receive 55 percent of the new company's effective output, including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. The official said the entity would be the second-largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco. But details remain scarce, and analysts have questioned the headline number. Oil market researcher Rory Johnston called the 65-billion-barrel figure 'a red herring' with little relevance to any actual deals, noting the real terms are still almost entirely unknown.
sections.whyItMatters: If realized, the arrangement would hand Washington a position over a vast portion of the world's proven reserves and a strategic hedge against the disruption of Gulf supply at a time when Hormuz traffic remains crippled by the Iran war. But the lack of fixed terms leaves its actual significance unclear — for now it is more spectacle than substance.

sections.heading: A Himalayan Glacial Collapse Becomes One of the Region's Deadliest Disasters
sections.body:
Catastrophic flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through communities along the Nepal-China border on Wednesday, killing more than 570 people and leaving nearly 2,000 missing, according to police and rescue officials cited by the Associated Press. The US Geological Survey said the flooding was triggered by a glacial collapse, and scientists' preliminary investigations point to rapidly melting Himalayan ice as the cause. CCTV footage showed a wall of water and mud several stories high sweeping through Gyirong Port near the border. Authorities warn of further flooding from a newly formed upstream lake, and about 90 US citizens remained unaccounted for as of Thursday.

The disaster has an unusually international dimension: people from more than 30 countries are among the missing, and South Korea has dispatched a rapid response team to Nepal as its citizens remain unaccounted for. Rescuers on both sides of the border are searching for survivors while bracing for the possibility of a second flood. Satellite imagery comparing the border region before and after Aug. 26 shows the scale of the devastation from the flash floods, which struck a border zone where China and Nepal must coordinate a cross-border response at a moment of heightened great-power tension.
sections.whyItMatters: The event underscores the accelerating risk of glacial lake outburst floods across the high Himalayas — a climate-driven hazard with cross-border implications for both China and Nepal, and for the communities and infrastructure along shared river systems. It is a humanitarian disaster unfolding at the intersection of climate change and great-power geopolitics.

sections.heading: The Ukraine War Intensifies on Both Ends of the Strike Map
sections.body:
The Russia-Ukraine war escalated in both directions this week. The UK deepened its direct role: Prime Minister Andy Burnham made Kyiv his first foreign trip on Monday, where Britain agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components of the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow with a range of about 240km — letting Ukraine manufacture the long-range missiles domestically. Moscow reacted sharply, with Kremlin adviser Andrei Fedorov telling the BBC he could not 'exclude 100 percent' that there might be 'semi-military' action against Britain, suggesting drone factories producing for Ukraine could come under attack from 'unknown sources.'

On the battlefield, the air war turned deadlier. The Wall Street Journal reports the air campaign over Ukraine has entered a more lethal phase, and AP says Ukraine has extended its long-range drone campaign into Russia, destroying a Wildberries logistics depot. A Russian strike on a weapons depot in the Kyiv area killed at least 37 people and forced hundreds to evacuate, with an investigation begun into the storage of weapons near a residential area. President Zelenskyy has warned, per CNN, that Russia is likely to mobilize at least 300,000 more troops, and Al Jazeera reports growing fears of a fresh Russian mobilization amid reports of intimidating recruitment tactics. The picture is of a war grinding toward a larger Russian escalation even as both sides keep a diplomatic door ajar.
sections.whyItMatters: By transferring missile production know-how, the UK is moving from supplying weapons to enabling Ukraine's domestic arms industry — a qualitative step Russia has explicitly framed as direct involvement. Combined with a possible new Russian mobilization and a more lethal air campaign, the window to shape the conflict's trajectory may be narrowing even as the CIA channel opens.

sections.heading: Sudan's War Spills Across Borders as Washington Pushes a Nationwide Embargo
sections.body:
Washington escalated its push to end Sudan's four-year war, pressing the UN Security Council to expand the country's arms embargo from Darfur to the entire nation. Trump's senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, Massad Boulos, told the Security Council on Monday that financial, military and political backing for both the government forces and the rival Rapid Support Forces remains a driver of the conflict, which has killed at least 59,000 people and displaced some 13 million. The proposed US resolution would apply the embargo to all parties operating in Sudan's territory and explicitly reaffirm that drones and related technologies fall under it. Boulos did not name the countries providing support, but AP notes Egypt has backed the military while UN experts and human rights groups have accused the UAE of arming the RSF, a charge Abu Dhabi denies.

The war is now spilling across borders. Chad accused Sudan's army of launching an air strike on a fuel market near their shared border that killed at least 12 people and wounded seven, with the US embassy in Khartoum backing Chad's account. The incident follows a Chadian claim last week that Sudan struck a military convoy more than 100km inside its territory. Chad has raised its alert level to its highest point and deployed about 100 armoured vehicles and signal-jamming trucks near the border. The strike threatens to draw a second state into a regional conflict that already destabilises the Sahel and the Red Sea approaches.
sections.whyItMatters: A nationwide embargo would be the first real attempt to cut the external arms flows that have kept Sudan's war grinding on, and it tests whether Washington can rally the Security Council on an African crisis while its attention is fixed on Iran. The spillover into Chad complicates that push and threatens to widen a conflict the UN warns threatens an entire generation.

bottomLine: The defining development of the week is the consolidation of the Iran war into an economic siege: six months in, with Hormuz closed and no off-ramp, Washington has pivoted from airstrikes to secondary sanctions that force every country to choose sides, even as Qatari, Omani and Pakistani mediators converge on Tehran and a direct US-Russia intelligence channel reopens. The war's hidden cost surfaced in a 'beyond critical' Patriot shortage that has hollowed out NATO's European missile defense. Around it, Washington spent the week rearranging its other relationships — a Venezuela oil deal that would hand it control of 65 billion barrels as a hedge against Hormuz, a trade war with Canada that escalated into renaming a shared lake, and a nationwide arms embargo push on Sudan as that war spills into Chad. A Himalayan glacial collapse killed more than 570, and the Ukraine air war turned deadlier even as the UK moved to enable domestic missile production. Going forward, the questions that matter are whether the economic siege on Iran breaks Tehran or hardens the standoff, whether Washington's parallel confrontations compound into overstretch, and whether the multiple diplomatic channels — Tehran, Moscow, Hormuz — produce anything concrete before the wars escalate further. The through-line is a Washington wielding economic and legal leverage aggressively against adversaries and allies alike, with no single decisive course yet committed.
sources: AP, BBC, Al Jazeera, Reuters, New York Times, Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, CNBC, CNN, PBS, Axios, France 24, Sky News, NPR, Türkiye Today, AzerNews, A News, US Treasury, UN
